claims.text: Adding yttrium to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance.
A yttrium addition of 0.1–1.0 at.% is an appropriate intervention range.
The proposed intervention applies to refractory high-entropy alloys in as-cast or wrought states.
The intervention should improve oxidation behavior during exposure at approximately 1000°C in air.
Yttrium alloying causes a protective yttrium oxide layer to form on the alloy surface.
The yttrium oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion through the surface scale reduces the oxidation rate.
Yttrium-alloyed material will have a lower oxidation rate than untreated refractory high-entropy alloy.
Yttrium-alloyed material will have a longer lifetime in oxidizing environments than untreated refractory high-entropy alloy.
The oxidation-resistance improvement should be significant above 900°C.
The oxidation-resistance improvement may be less pronounced below 900°C.
Refractory high-entropy alloys are candidates for ultrahigh-temperature structural applications.
The optimal yttrium concentration and precise oxidation-resistance mechanism are not well established.
Untreated and yttrium-alloyed alloys should be compared after exposure at 1000°C in air for approximately 100 hours.
Oxidation rate, scale thickness, and microstructure should be measured in the comparison.
The hypothesis is falsified if the yttrium-alloyed alloy does not show significantly lower oxidation rate and scale thickness than the untreated control.
